items.title: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers. Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. items.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
items.excerpt: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! Tags: firefox, html, mozilla, datasette

items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.excerpt: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted: I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting.so(or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did: Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report. Tags: c, research, sqlite, rust, claude

items.title: Mini Brains, Beating Heart Organoids, and the AI That Predicts Them — Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: Biohub, Google, Meta, DOE, and NIH have announced a $1.8B initiative to make biology predictable, with new technologies to measure living systems across molecular scales, space, and time. But why now? Despite training foundation models on hundreds of millions of cells, researchers still struggle to predict what happens when we perturb them. Sometimes even simple linear models or mean predictions are surprisingly difficult to beat. Is the problem the models, the benchmarks, or the biological questions we're asking? We sat down with Fabian Theis, Director of the Computational Health Center at Helmholtz Munich, whose lab helped build Scanpy and scverse and has pioneered models of cellular behavior. We explore Nicheformer, scConcept, CellFlow, and LabCompass, following the progression from mapping cells to predicting their responses and ultimately designing experiments to control their behavior. Along the way, we discuss the Bitter Lesson in biology, the controversial Arc Virtual Cell Challenge, modeling multicellular systems, the business of virtual cells, and why closing the lab-in-the-loop may be as much an organizational challenge as a computational one. items.title: How Salesforce uses Claude Code
items.author: Claude
items.excerpt: Salesforce scaled Claude Code to thousands of engineers and doubled effective output, with fewer bugs per line of code than before. Engineering leaders from Salesforce explain how they measure AI coding ROI with an "effective output" score built with Stanford researchers, and how an agent maturity curve moved engineers from simple prompts to autonomous agents across the software development life cycle. They also cover a decades-old codebase made headless in weeks instead of a year, a marketplace for sharing agent skills, incident agents that find the right team automatically, and a bug that Claude Opus tracked down in 24 hours after human attempts failed. items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: Will Anthropic make it from filing an S-1 to trading on Nasdaq? Jamin Ball, partner at Altimeter and author of Clouded Judgement, joins swyx to walk through the roadshow, the Thanksgiving window and what investors would need to believe about Claude. Jamin makes a case for going public that starts with the lenders financing GPU clusters. Then he opens the accounts: in the first half of 2026, Anthropic reported an $80.7 billion net loss and generated $3.9 billion in operating cash. He explains how the rising value of shares promised to early investors flows through the income statement, and why he watches the cost of serving Claude alongside revenue growth. items.title: GitHub’s Growth: 225M Developers, 34.3B Commits — Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI, Microsoft
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: GitHub’s next scaling challenge is the agent workload. The platform has 225 million developers and handled 34.3 billion commits over the past year. Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI at Microsoft, joins us straight after his GitHub Universe keynote to talk about rebuilding the software-development stack for that scale. We get into Copilot Fusion’s approach to model orchestration and the quality–cost frontier; the harness underneath it; agents that carry a session across phone, desktop and VS Code; and the infrastructure work behind GitHub’s move to Azure. Jay also makes the case for measuring AI spending against completed work and business outcomes. Along the way: why Jay skips pull requests in some of his own repos, Matt Pocock’s repo of Markdown instructions, and the open-source maintenance question behind replacing 2,000 dependencies with 20. Stay for the programmable conference badge at the end.
